chunks: "Short version: divide by the resistor. If I measure 20 millivolts across a 10 milliohm sense resistor, the current is 20 millivolts divided by 10 milliohms, which is 2 amps.
On the scope I would either do that division in my head, set the channel's units or scale so the screen reads amps directly, or use a math channel that divides channel 1 by 0. 01.
But there are a few things I check so I trust it. First, where is the resistor? If it is on the low side, one end is ground, so a normal probe works.
If it is on the high side, both ends are floating above ground, so I need a differential probe, or two probes subtracted, which is much less accurate.
Second, the voltage is small, so I put the probe on the resistor's own pads, turn on bandwidth limit to cut noise, and keep the vertical scale tight enough to use the ADC range.
Third, the resistor has tolerance and some inductance, so for fast edges the waveform can show spikes that are really L di/dt, not current.
If that matters, I cross-check with a current probe or a DMM in series."
